analysis.one_liner: Taxes stock, bond, and derivative trades to fund public investment, reimbursing small investors.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would tax stock trades at 0.5% and derivatives at 0.005%, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee in June 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a small tax on purchases of financial assets: 0.5% of the value of a stock trade, 0.1% on bonds, and 0.005% on derivatives, collected by exchanges and brokers rather than individual investors. New stock issues, very short-term debt, and routine securities lending would be exempt. Households earning under $50,000 ($75,000 for couples) could claim a credit reimbursing any of the tax they pay, so the cost would fall mainly on frequent and high-volume traders. The revenue would fund the priorities named in the bill's title, including families, infrastructure, and the environment.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, ordinary taxpayers would gain revenue for public programs without paying the tax themselves in most cases: the credit would fully reimburse the tax for eligible individuals with income under $50,000 ($75,000 joint), exempting initial stock offerings protects companies raising capital, and the exemptions for short-term debt and securities lending protect normal market plumbing. The tax is designed to fall hardest on high-frequency and high-volume traders, for whom a fraction of a percent per trade is material, while having little effect on a household that trades occasionally.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers; public programs funded by trading tax

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 0.5% tax on stock purchases, 0.1% on bond purchases, and 0.005% on derivatives, with the tax paid by exchanges and brokers rather than individual investors, so no household has to file or pay it directly.

Gives an income tax credit that reimburses eligible individuals for any financial transaction tax they paid, but only for those earning under $50,000 a year ($75,000 for joint filers), with the threshold indexed to inflation — concentrating the burden on wealthier investors.

Exempts initial stock and bond offerings (so companies raising capital are not taxed), very short-term debt maturing in 60 days or less, and standard securities lending, limiting the tax to secondary-market trading.
Covers digital assets and includes anti-avoidance rules directing the Treasury to write regulations preventing traders from escaping the tax by routing transactions through non-U.S. persons.
Directs the revenue toward the purposes stated in the bill: investing in families and communities, infrastructure, the environment, and financial security, and reducing market volatility.

analysis.who_pays: The direct cost falls on buyers of financial assets and the institutions that execute their trades: exchanges and brokers must collect and remit the tax, and high-frequency trading firms, hedge funds, banks, and active asset managers would pay it on every covered purchase. Part of the cost would be passed on indirectly to investors generally, including people with retirement accounts, through slightly higher trading costs — and households above the credit's income cap would have no offset at all.
analysis.who_pays_short: Frequent traders, banks, hedge funds, exchanges

drawbacks.text: The tax would be passed through to ordinary savers in one important way: index funds, mutual funds, and pension funds that trade on behalf of investors would bear the tax, and people whose savings sit in those funds receive no credit — the credit only reaches individuals who are the beneficial owner of the security and earn under $50,000 ($75,000 joint), so a retiree with a 401(k) earning modest income from Social Security plus a pension could exceed the cap and eat the cost with no offset.

Taxing derivatives at 0.005% of the value of the underlying investment, and treating each swap or options payment as a separate taxable transaction, creates a large new information-reporting and collection job for the IRS in coordination with the SEC and CFTC, with administrative costs that an honest supporter would have to weigh against the revenue.

Because only purchases are taxed, trading could shift to foreign venues or be restructured to avoid the tax; the bill directs Treasury to write anti-avoidance regulations covering non-U.S. parties, but how tightly those rules could close the door is untested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is designed to put the burden where its sponsors intended — on high-volume, speculative trading — while reimbursing low- and middle-income individuals directly, which is more protection than most financial transaction tax proposals offer. The real weak points are the pass-through of the tax to anyone invested in funds, who gets no credit regardless of income, and the administrative burden of taxing every derivatives payment. As a revenue measure with a redistributive credit, it is reasonably designed; the open questions are how much revenue it would actually collect after avoidance and how much compliance friction it adds.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the tax-writing committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Barbara Lee of California introduced the bill on June 14, 2023, joined by 13 original cosponsors including Pramila Jayapal and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez; all cosponsors were Democrats.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that handles tax legislation.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-frequency trading firms, banks, hedge funds, and the exchanges that would have collected the tax are better off, because no tax on their transactions was ever enacted. Nothing changed for ordinary taxpayers either, since the revenue the bill would have raised never materialized.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wall Street trading firms, banks, and exchanges

for.name: Rep. Barbara Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 13 original cosponsors from the progressive wing of the House Democratic caucus.

for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Jayapal, Ocasio-Cortez, McGovern, and Schakowsky

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral on June 14, 2023 — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Held the House majority and controlled the floor calendar in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: With Republicans holding a majority and no Republican support for the bill, it had no path to the floor even had it cleared committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported the bill; the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee never acted on it, and no vote of any kind was ever recorded.

industries.note: A tax on every covered purchase strikes hardest at firms trading in and out of positions thousands of times a day, which is precisely the behavior the bill's title targets as speculation. Stopping the bill preserved their business model and cost structure unchanged.

The bill makes exchanges located in the United States the collectors of the tax on trades executed or cleared on their facilities, adding compliance obligations and raising the cost of trading on U.S. venues.

industries.industry: Banks, hedge funds, and asset managers
industries.note: Institutions buying stocks, bonds, and derivatives would pay the tax on each purchase, with no credit available since credits go only to eligible individuals. Some of the cost would be passed on to fund investors, including retirement savers.

Brokers would be responsible for collecting and remitting the tax on trades they execute and reporting covered-transaction information to the IRS, a new compliance burden; their cost-conscious retail customers under the income cap would be reimbursed through the credit.
